"Like some other (amazing) rogue-ish games that started out in Early Access and successfully launched, Risk of Rain 2 really stands out among all of the other games available out there. From the intense gameplay loop to the delightful art style to the absolutely phenomenal evolving soundtrack, RoR2 pulls no punches. I bought RoR2 fairly early into EA, but the recent 1.0 update has forced my hand and I finally had to write some words on this incredibly enjoyable game.  To put it simply: Risk of Rain 2 is a scaling race against the increasingly difficult procedural generation AI. Everything gets crazier and crazier, going from fighting simple small beetles that prance towards you at the beginning of a run, all the of way to otherworldly stilted mechs that explode into black holes. The three regular difficulty settings adjust the speed and intensity that this difficulty mechanic spirals out of control.  On the highest of these settings you are forced into dancing a fine line around playing as fast as you can versus how fully you explore each map. Exploration is the key to victory as your main mechanic of scaling is opening randomly sprawled chests and hoping that you get something that helps your current situation. Yet time is against you once again, and these chests get increasingly more expensive (cash drops from kills) as the clock ticks on. One run you might be a god of destruction, setting off chain reactions of explosive death over an entire map with homing spectral knives; another you could be blitzing across levels at ludicrous speeds avoiding everything in your path on the way to the exit portal. The developers understand, so instead Risk of Rain 2 asks, ""But why not both?""."

Un juego que empieza muy bien y pincha a la mitad de muy mala manera.  Al princpio, el juego apunta maneras: Somos un soldado americano que se mete en una instalación científica rusa abandonada para investigarla, y por unos problemas se queda solo. Nos tocará explorar la zona y enseguida encontraremos que aquí el tiempo funciona de manera extraña. Encontraremos un dispositivo de control temporal, pasillos por los que avanzar y enemigos a los que matar por el camino.  Recuerda mucho a Half-Life 1 y 2 en su desarrollo y estructura (Gravity gun incluida), su armamento y los tipos de enemigos que nos encontramos. Dicen que también se parece a Bioshock, pero a mí no me lo pareció.  Vamos, que hasta ahí me gustaba lo que me encontraba. Poca variedad de enemigos, pero compensada con un buen ritmo y diseño de niveles, que aseguraban una variedad de situaciones decente incluso con esa limitación, y buenos cambios entre exploración, puzzles y combate, algunos de ellos muy trepidantes y con dificultad bien ajustada, necesitando gestionar la munición y manejar diferentes armas.  Desgraciadamente, todo eso cambia a partir de la mitad del juego (la escena del tren).   No sé qué pasaría, pero a partir de ahí la dificultad se vuelve inexistente (Subimos de nivel muy rápido y tenemos munición para aburrir), dejan de salir nuevos enemigos, no hay apenas combates y es todo tirar p'alante, ni siquiera puzzles, y la historia/ambientación del juego no me parece lo bastante fuerte para poder aguantar todo lo demás por sí sola...  En resumen, un juego que se quedó a medias, por el motivo que fuese. Una pena.

In many ways this is actually really cool - but it's also very frustrating to realise that you've played through, and, that's it, especially with a relatively high price.  However, this game has some beautiful polish, design, pixel art, and the interface systems for the creature's tentacles make for a genuinely different control scheme and play style - so, short as it is, this is a perfect game to pick up on sale, or when you need a break from more standard fare.

I picked this up on a whim (75% off), and was pleased with it. I don't really care for elaborate reviews, so I'll keep it simple.  THE GOOD: -The soundtrack is awesome. These feel like tunes that would've been stuck in my head from 1991. -The weapon upgrade system is neat. It allows you to really tailor your approach. -The gameplay. This is pretty solid Metroidvania. -Linear difficulty curve. For an afternoon play, I got enough challenging spots without getting frustrated.  THE NOT-SO-GOOD: -The weapon upgrade system. 3 of your 5 upgrades are worthless. Faster projectiles, maybe. But the angled shots? Why bother. Wave shot was helpful for exactly 1 enemy in the game. -Storyline. There isn't one. -The backtracking. Metroidvania-style games are notorious for this. However, the upgrades you get are used in every single level. So it's essentially trial-and-error to find the level that you can progress the furthest in with the set of upgrades you have. -The same creature is used for every single boss fight. Enemies are recycled in every single level. -The levels look different, but ultimately play out exactly the same. -The game is very short. I registered 4.9 hours, and that's only because I spent a good chunk of that making dinner and watching TV with my girlfriend. -A lot of wasted potential.

Nos encontramos ante un juego 'point & click' sobre una novela de Agatha Christie, con personajes muy bien caracterizados y con un buen estilo, la cosa promete, mola eso de ser Poirot, pero eh... no es oro todo lo que reluce, y diré por qué:  -El juego es MUY corto, dura unas horas de sufrimiento por el siguiente apartado.  -Es MUY lento, por ratos desquiciante, tanto en saltos 'post cinemáticas' como en su movilidad e interación, obligandote muchas veces a hacer cosas e ir a sitios que están a la vuelta de la esquina pero entre una cosa y otra te tiras unos minutos en hacer nada.  -La dificultad es páuperrima, para estar hablando de un juego basado en una novela detectivesca con mayúsculas con nombre y caché de primer orden, los puzzles son de broma, las pistas vienen dadas y todo en sí es facilisimo, solo tienes que pasar el ratón por encima de algo y te dirá que puedes hacer, vamos... una novela visual de corte manual, debería apuntarse como nueva etiqueta de producto.  -Las formas de deducción están relativamente bien, son novedosas, pero vamos, seguimos en lo mismo, que no tiene dificultad, puedes equivocarte que lo único que vas a perder es, tiempo; de hecho muchas veces sabes más de lo que te permiten hacer, obligandote a seguir unas pautas cuando sabes que alguien aún así no pinta nada en la investigación. Y es así, porque el juego no da para más, porque es muy simple, si no, hubiera varios caminos, formas de jugar, opciones de algún tipo o desenlaces, pero no, esto es claramente una firme novela visual de escasa dificultad.  - Este juego no debería valer más de un euro, pero vale 4,50, rebajado de ->14,99<-, lo siento por quienes hayáis gastado esa cantidad, a ami me parece muy abusiva para tan poco entretenimiento y contenido, la calidad/precio no lo vale.  - No lo recomiendo, es un gasto de dinero inutil que se puede invertir en otros juegos que sí aportan diversión, este lo único que aporta es, pasar el rato, gastar el tiempo, conocer la novela si no la leíste (que no es poco).

The original Left 4 Dead was a co-op experience that many gamers felt couldn't be beaten. When Left 4 Dead 2 was announced, there was a push from gamers to simply add the content to the original game and not make a second iteration. What they didn't know is how much more you would be able to do with the second game.  Left 4 Dead 2 is one of the best co-op/single player experiences I've had to date. The Steam version of the game is the only way to go, as you get all of the DLC for free along with the campaigns from the first Left 4 Dead. The different game modes keep the gameplay fresh and new almost every time you play. From the story mode where you are fighting to get from safe room to safe room, to the online play where two teams of four take turns playing as the survivors and the infected, the game simply doesn't have an equal as far as content - and the cost of entry is extremely low.   Costing 20$ on the digital market on Xbox Live, you will still need to pay more for all of the DLC, costing anywhere from ten to fifteen dollars per pack. The steam version is 20$ normally (the game was free just a few days ago, not to mention the lowered cost every time there is a Steam sale) and you get all of the DLC FOR FREE. This is a game that simply can't be beaten. If you are into first person shooters, or even just zombie games in general, you need to get this game ASAFP.

Having played through the base game, Spacechem is a great puzzle game at it's core.   Pros - The puzzles. They become increasing harder as you go along, but it is pretty steady. Each set of puzzles build on skills you have acquired from the previous. There are challenges associated with many of the puzzles. You do not have to complete them to beat the game, but they really make you think and work for the achievement. They can be tough, but I enjoyed solving them. Nothing in the game is forced on you with the challenges and achievements. It saves your progress so you can keep moving forward in the game and go back later to beat the challenges. I really felt a sense of accomplishment finishing this game. Many puzzle games become the a+b =c formula and thus, boring. Space Chem held to the end.  The controls and UI worked really well. Learning the hotkeys helps. There are many videos on You Tube. Really cool after you beat a puzzle, you can see how others did it. I did not see any of my solutions online and there are may ways to solve each one. The instruction on new tools were good. Told you what you needed to know and left you to figure out how to employ them. The periodic chart was a useful addition.  Cons – The story outside the puzzles was a cheese sandwich with the crust (Try eating one and you'll see what I mean, dry and chewy, just sayin'). Not the worst I have seen, but after while I didn't bother. I mention this only to point out it does not take away from the great puzzles. That is the heart of this great gem. If you don't like the story, skip it. The graphics do not interfere with the game at all. They were functional.   I highly recommend this game if you enjoy puzzles that challenge your critical thinking and problem solving abilities. This is an exceptional game. Skip the story, solve the puzzles. You'll feel smarter, I do.

Right now Steam cites me at about 30 hours. In reality I've probably plunked down double that while not connected to Steam. There are a lot of reviews that read like kids looking for a quick giggle, which is understandable. But this game strikes a heavy chord for anyone who is old enough to remember the Cold War.  This game is, in a word, sobering. It is incredibly simplistic, the controls are very basic, and the gameplay doesn't change much. I kind of doubt the production team was attempting to build as complete a simulator as they did because if I were sitting in NORAD and lighting off Peacekeepers and scrambling Stratofortresses, I would imagine it would feel a bit like this. The ambience of the game is probably the most unnerving part of immersion. Hearing people sobbing and coughing while you're watching nuclear warheads pass each other over the polar cap does something to you.    The real upshot to the game was multiplayer, especially with randos. Unfortunately the multiplayer landscape for the game tends to be unpopulated due to the age of the game and more addictive (and casual fun) games like LoL.   I would suggest buying this game if you are looking for something that you can play with a friend or two and aren't looking to break the bank. The AI is good to teach you the basics, but very predictable. Be sure everyone understands how to speed up the game, too, and you can do 45-60 minute matches.

I basically deleted my original review solely to cover a new topic:  Paid mods.  First of all, it was bound to happen at some point. And like Steam market itself, it was always expected and even probably justified that Bethesda would take a cut of each paid mod. While this is disappointing for lots of folks, and understandably so, it was bound to happen at some point.  Secondly: did it have to be added after-the-fact, though, to a game that didn't originally launch with paid mods? That's the part where I do tend to agree with a lot of the players complaining. Creation Club is, in itself, just the next logical step for where modding is going. But, why retroactively add Creation Club to games that didn't launch with them? That was always a 100% lock as far as irritating the folks who bought those games at a time when nothing at all was said about turning mods into a paid-DLC sort of format.  Third: I highly suspect two things played into shoe-horning in Creation Club to FO4. The first is that FO4 disappointed a good chunk of the playerbase that always came to FO for the roleplay: losing some of the playerbase in this manner likely hurt the DLC sales and encouraged a quicker implementation of Creation Club, as opposed to adding it in to whatever game comes next for Bethesda. The second factor, then, was probably that they feared starting Creation Club with the very next game would cripple sales... better to experiment with it in a game that already sold whatever it was going to sell, then to possibly wreck future sales on a new title.   Overall, the game itself has its flaws, but has enough positives (technical stability, crafting, solid combat, more interesting environment design than FO:NV) that I feel it's worth recommending. The roleplay is a giant step back, and dialogue choices are poor, and quest design is sometimes less flexible than FO:NV, but overall it's a decent game.  As far as the Creation Club, too: it's not like they took the console away. You can still get by playing around a bit on your own, and unlike some games I've played (Total War: Rome 2, namely), it's not like I feel mods are needed just to get a reasonable experience playing.  All of this said, though, yes, Creation Club feels pretty sleazy when tagged onto a game that didn't launch with it, didn't advertise implementing it at some future point, and doesn't seem entirely fair to implement well after-the-fact. Even then, there were clues along the way that this might be coming (the GECK and other issues that came up point to this).   TL;DR - Creation Club is the next logical step for modding. At some point, mods were eventually going to find a way to become a money-maker for both the modders and the publishers, as one provides the original assets and software and the other uses that stuff to make improved content. My only gripe is that Creation Club really shouldn't have been added to an existing game that I bought before such a massive change/feature was made. But I think I know why Creation Club was shoe-horned in, but you'll have to read the actual review for that discussion.  Again, game is actually pretty good, official DLC is largely acceptable, but Creation Club should have been left to wait until the next Bethesda game, rather than tacked-on.

This game looks gorgeous and tries to expand on its mechanics in varied and interesting ways.  However, I have a hard time reconciling the demanding and arbitrary goals with the frustrating movement in a way that provides enjoyment. Slingshotting my spaceship around a moon should feel exhilarating rather than tedious. To the extent that this game succeeds as a series of puzzles to be solved, it also fails by making the execution of solutions a bore to carry out, robbing the player of any joy in their triumph. On top of this gameplay loop, the after-mission scoring punishes the player for not conserving enough fuel/succeeding quickly enough/etc. The idea of playing through the same mission again to conserve an extra one percent of my fuel is painful enough to make me turn back from the game completely, and the promise of trudging through another solution is not intriguing enough to keep me moving forward.

Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon Wildlands review by Kurz  For Onono - Gamers Connect. All reviews is also available at: https://www.onono.no/   10/10   Introduction  Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon Wildlands, by Ubisoft Paris and published by Ubisoft, was released on March 7, 2017. Wildlands is the 10th game in the series but the first Ghost Recon game to go with the open world concept. It is one of the biggest open world maps that Ubisoft has ever created.   Gameplay  The game starts off in the high mountains of Bolivia. At first, you get drawn into the awesome graphics that surround you, complete with detailed and nicely made terrain, trees, grass, and so on. It’s purely breathtaking. When you start off, you get three bots to play with, or you can choose to play with friends in co-op. If you choose to play in coop, the bots will disappear. Ghost Recon Wildlands is played in a 3rd person perspective, but you have the option of taking on a first person view as well. You play as a member of the Delta Company, and your task is to retake control of Bolivia. Your target is the druglord El Sueño, who is running the biggest drug cartel in the world, and it’s up to you and or your friends to take him Down.  There are different difficulties you can put on to make the game easy or extremely challenging. I would recommend putting it has high as you can tolerate, since it will increase the amount of fun you have in the game. There is nothing like sneaking up to a base and silently take out the entire force who are armed with a high skill set. I would recommend if you are playing with friends that you put your difficulties at the same as your friends. That will force you to play the same tactics.  Doing missions in the dark compared to daytime makes a big difference in how you plan your entry. During the night, you have the advantage of stealth. Many of the soldiers are also sleeping during the night, making them an easy target. Drones are your best friend in the game. You can easily scout an entire base within a minute to plan your attack. The first of the drones have fewer abilities, but as you progress and get the experience required, you can upgrade your drone to be quicker and stronger.  There is a wide variety of weapons, clothing, and ways to customize your equipment. Ghost Recon Wildlands uses weapons from different militaries around the world. As you progress in your game, you will find and unlock new guns, add-ons, clothing, and vehicles. Helicopter is my main way of transportation, and the sweet thing is that you can spawn in any vehicle wherever you are on the map, making it easy to travel. You can also teleport to different locations you have unlocked on the map, or you can teleport to any of your friends.  The map is huge and is divided into 21 areas. The different areas have different difficulties, meaning it’s best to start out with the lower levels. When you enter a new area, you unlock new missions to complete. The missions in the different areas are controlled by a Buchon, and to progress towards eliminating them, you need to take out the underbosses.  Cutscenes for the story are well made, and Karen Bowman is as bad as you can get. Spoiler alert: pressuring cartel members to overdose on coke to makes them squeal.  Special Operations Ubisoft has done a lot to support the game over the years. They have made several special operations to keep players like me playing the game continuously.  There are currently five special operations:  Predator Operation Watchman Operation Archangel Operation Silent Spade Operation Oracle   DLC  There are 2 DLCs for Ghost Recon Wildlands: Narco Road and Fallen Ghosts. They both take place on self-sustaining maps- both edited parts of the original map. The gameplay is a little bit different from the original game, but they both have some interesting new implements. For example, the way your vehicles and planes are made so much more arcade-like in Narco Road to the awesome new enemies you encounter in Fallen Ghost. I would recommend them both, but I wish they had made the DLCs’ maps expand into the main map.   Conclusion  If you want to get an awesome shooter game with cooperative gameplay, there is no way around Ghost Recon Wildlands. It is the best Coop game out there to date, even if it’s some years old. The world of Wildlands is so beautiful, you can just drive around enjoying the view. 10/10   Pros  - Amazing open world - Fun to play with friends - Almost unlimited ways to edit guns, skins and clothing - Long campaign - Great story   Cons  - Helicopters may spawn but not where you wanted - DLCs are not an extension of the original map - You need a lot of free time to play it - Can be repetitive to some degree - Desolated places have little content   Written by Kurz   Please follow our reviewer`s at our Steam Curator page: http://store.steampowered.com/curator/31367524/  Our link to Friend & Foe in discord is: https://discord.gg/32Hn7ZV Steam group link: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/friendandfoe

Castle of Illusion tem um lugar especial em minha memória. Foi o primeiro jogo de Master System que eu zerei e o Primeiro de Mega Drive que eu joguei/zerei.  Quando foi anunciado o remake de Castle of Illusion fiquei bem empolgado, mas ao ver que ai ser em 3D eu fiquei com o pé atrás já que a maioria dos remakes de jogos 2D feitos em 3D não me agradaram por fugir demais do que era o original.  Em Castle of Illusion os caras acertaram em cheio na forma de transpor o original 2D para 3D. O jogo ficou com gráficos e trilha sonora maravilhosa sem perder a essência da jogabilidade original. Aliás todas as fases tem um bocado de elementos adicionados em relação ao original mas em completa sintonia com o que já existia. A jogabilidade é majoritariamente 2D, e mesmo nos pequenos trechos onde a jogabilidade passa de 2D para 3D, ficou muito bacana.  Como no original o jogo é fácil e curto, mas nessa versão tem o adicional de completar 100% do jogo coletando todos os itens (para quem curte esse tipo de coisa) o que extende um pouco mais o jogo. Eu joguei ele com calma olhando cenários e explorando um bocado e prestando atenção nos detalhes e mesmo assim demorei menos de 3 horas para salvar a Minnie e 7,5hrs pra completar 100% do jogo. O povo mais apressado vai fazer ambos em bem menos tempo.  O único ponto onde acho que podiam ter feito melhor foi na introdução e final... ao invés das imagens estáticas, deveriam ter usado a própria engine 3D do jogo nelas e as feito totalmente animadas. Ou ainda melhor... ter feito elas em animação no estilo da Disney, ou mesmo feito pela própria Disney. Ai teria ficado perfeito. Mesmo assim ainda acho que o jogo merece nota 10/10.  Recomendado para todos. Obrigatório pra quem é fã do jogo original.

Fantastic 4x game. I can't tell you the number of hours I've sunk into this title.  (I owned this game long before it was available on steam.)  Pros: Truly massive empires - On the larger settings you can fight for control of hundreds of star systems, each with potentially a dozen or more planets.  Tons of empires - not only can your empires be big, but there can be a LOT of them. I've had games with as many as thirty separate empires competing with each other. Deep Customization - You have the ability to change every aspect of your empire, from how fast they are able to repair ships to how well ground troops fair in combat. You get to choose the type of atmosphere your species breaths, and even which unique tech or traits they possess. (Are you mechanoids immune to plagues? Are you natural merchants? etc) Complete ship customization - You assemble ships module by module. Similar to Endless Space, but vastly more detailed.  Tons of weapons and technologies - the tech tree is vast, and there a ton of weapon types. You can focus on missiles, torpedos, beams, high-energy discharge, weapon disabling, shield disruption, phased weapon, etc. The list goes on. (Not to mention troops, mines, and fighters.)  Cons: Graphics: are serviceable, but nothing to write home about. Interface: Difficult to understand when you are first beginning. Not too bad once you get the hang of it. Diplomacy: This is the one area where SEIV struggles; diplomatic options are not well described, and nor well fleshed out. However, you can make enemy empires protectorates and stuff, so that's a nice touch.  Overall, I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of Turn Based 4x games.

I don’t understand why many people suggest this game, probably because of its similarity to Mount and Blade. I understand the excitement. I feel that too, but it does not mean that the concept of Mount and Blade is implemented properly. The game lacks some fundamental things to be a full version. Be warned the game still looks, feels, and is an early-access. There are tons of things that have to be improved greatly for decent gameplay. In its current state, it may be playable for some but it annoys me a lot because faults are very simple and fundamental things that any published game should get right if the game is not a tech-demo or a school project. Given that it’s sold for £22.99 in its current state, it is way too expensive and obviously does not deserve that price. Wait for the sale and the future updates.   Good things about the game that I have encountered around 2 hours gameplay: -Battles feel nice. I like the fact that my sword does not get stuck in enemy’s body. -Commanding your troops is very intuitive when you got right how the system works.  -The campaign looks promising. -Many different maps are a bonus. -Fairly well optimized but still needs to get much work done.  Bad things about the game, unfortunately, weigh more: -Scaling is clearly not right. My in-game hands are massive. I feel like I am a giant in the game. -Gameplay mechanics are horribly implemented: --Handling weapons is very poor. Even there is a lag in holding animation. Sometimes swords float in my hand.   --Throwing is a disaster. Items go unintended places unbelievably fast. --‘Ragdoll physics’ looks and feels nice, but it is rather jelly physics. When I hit hard enemies, they get spaghettified. -Sounds are horrible. I don’t expect perfect sound effects from an indie game. Since they charge AA title price, so I have the right to expect decent quality sound effects or forget about quality but sound effects themselves. At least please add the basic ones. For example, there is no sound effect when you draw an arrow from the quiver. how the heck am I supposed to understand if I grab it or not? -Menu, Interface and in-game texts are repulsive. They have the appearance of late 90s games. Clearly it wasn’t the developers’ priority. But especially texts should have been a priority because we are supposed to read many texts hours and hours. -There is no health or armour bar. Neither proper damage indicator. During the battle, you have to guess how much damage you got. I don’t count b&w screen because it does not tell me how much damage I could get before I die.  Unfortunately, this promising title does not present a decent gameplay in 2020. It might have been a gem before other well-developed and developing vr games. I hope the future updates will iron out small but glaring issues and polish the game eventually. I will for sure update the review then.

Classic Doom with a twist. I'm tempted to say vets only, since it gets quite difficult very early on if you're playing on Watch Me Die like you're supposed to, especially as this was originally meant for the N64 controller. The puzzle and navigation elements are the most complicated in the entire series too. They really went to town on the puzzles nearer the end.  Some of the level design is second only to Knee Deep in the Dead. If it wasn't for the absence of certain enemies and the original HUD (more on that later), this would be my favourite official Doom game. I'm not sure I'd call this a sequel like some do, as it is certainly a spinoff, but it's a wonderful spinoff and ESSENTIAL playing for anyone who has beaten Doom II on UV. It's great to have another Doom game aside from 1 and 3 to focus on atmosphere.  I would've liked some of the cut monsters to be thrown in as their absence was really felt towards the end of the game, but the designers did really well with what they had. Whoever came up with the idea of a twin-mouthed Pain Elemental should be shot, especially as the Lost Souls seem to be buffed with massively increased speed and attack strength with slightly less defence. That might be an attempt to balance out the lack of Arch-Viles and Revenants. I also would have liked for more animations, especially for the SSG, which feels really weird at first after playing Doom II for years. I also miss the old HUD, and wish it became more standard in FPS games - I would like to see what weapons I have along with quantities of ammo without having to switch weapon.  (How did people play this with a controller? Respect, my brothers.)  Edit: Yay I beat the game! 12 hours for a 100%-ish run. Here is my controversial new tier list: (Almost perfect) Doom II Doom Eternal Doom 64 Doom  Doom 3 Final Doom Doom 2016 (Great)  Yup. It's that good. I've dived into The Lost Levels and they're clearly made for keyboard and mouse players, while making the most out of the original assets without the limitations of N64 hardware. I'm really enjoying them.

Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is the fifth installment in the Saints Row series. It centers on Johnny Gat and his adventures through hell, which in this case is a remake of Steelport full of Satan's minions. It's basically like Saints Row IV but with minions instead of aliens. It is considerably shorter, but enjoyable if you're a fan. It does not surpass Saints Row IV, nor Saints Row The Third, because unlike this one, those two are highly replayable. This one is not so much. Once you're finished with it you don't exactly feel like playing anymore, mostly because Hell is not a nice place to stay. Just wow. This game is such an amazing and unusual experience. A grim detective story with such a vivid characters, voice acting and visual style. This is a great game, which contsits a half of exploration and a half of interactive movie. Exploration, even if limited, is done in really interesting plain - you're a ghost, and thus you can walk through walls, collect and read ghostly notes and hints, learn about places and their stories. You will investigate some simple problems by collecting evidence, looking and listening. The 'movie' part is done nice. The plot is pretty interesting, although so simple. Sometimes I was wondering, when my character will figure out the killer. I mean, I partly looked through it before the game called the killer. However even by figuring out what was happening I've never seen who exactly was the one to blame. And there was yet another unexpected twist. So even if plot is slightly predictable, It's written dam-good. Definitely a movie I liked to play. I loved cats in this game. Just like cats should be in games. Fast, black, agile, a little glitchy. What I didn't like about them was how people react them. Like zero F-s were given that night. I loved that monitor reference in police station. You'll know when you see it. Square Enix, oh you. Now to the downsides: 1. This is a game best played with a gamepad. I mean it. It wasn't made to be on PC, it was made to be cross-platform. So even if it supports keyboard+mouse, use a controller, if you have one. 2. There is no free roam after you've reached the last checkpoint. The main menu will offer you to continue, but this is merely a last checkpoint, no way to collect something you've left for later. 3. Not sure about the reason, but sometimes I've experienced minor graphic glitches while ui showed/hided collected piece of evidence. Might be just my laptop. 4. Repetative faces of pedestrians. There's something like two or three models for each gender. Nuff said. 5. Really strange placement of hiding spots. Some places have plenty of them, but never needed. The others feature but a few spots, but you will need more if you need them. And some are too far to jump between them. 6. Font. Handwriting fonts in games never work as easy-to-read fonts. And this game has tons of handwritten text. Although I managed to read without problems, some might have them.  But in the end, I really enjoyed this game. It's certainly a great experience.

Having now 100% completed this game, achievements, collectibles, and all, I feel I can safely say that it is not quite worth /that/ amount of effort. That said, it's a fun stealth/action game that has very nicely set up its playstyle-reward system in a way that incentivizes playing through the few levels more than once without punishing you for having a favorite way of clearing a stage.  I, for one, love trying for the non-lethal ghost runs, and there are bonus points for both facets of that style of play. However, I did enjoy going back through the levels (of which, sadly, there are really only two or three, with slight variations in where you can and need to go each time through) for the speed runs or collection-quest side objectives that gave me a chance to mess around with some of the game's lethal options or see just how many guards I could get on my tail without dying to a hail of throwing knives.  The enemy AI is a bit spotty, the beetle and Orc enemies are absolute pains in the ass at times, and more than once I screwed myself over when Styx auto-grabbed onto a ledge or climbed up an edge I'd wanted to hang off of. These are problems that generally don't /ruin/ the experience so much as discolor it slightly. If you're smart with your quick-saving - and don't mind the moderately long loading times that quick-loading can bring - they'll be little more than minor setbacks.  For comparisons, think of it like Assassin's Creed without a lot of its fluff, or like a very mobile, third-person Thief game. Glitchy, a bit frustrating at times, but fun and rewarding from the get-go in spite of its flaws.

Sword Coast Legends (Time in Game Head Start 54 hrs)  Pre-purchasing the game, I have been around since Head Start 1 in which time there has been extremely little added to this game.    Issues:  - DM tools very limited  - No Tile by Tile dungeon Creation  - No DM Craftable or Placeable Weapons,   - All Loot is Random  - Modules created by DM tools are extrememly linear with no DM as there is no scripting  - No Branching Dialouge options in DM tools  - Single Player Campaign is very linear  - Character Graphics are rough and Blocky  - Skill trees really kill the D&D feel  - Wizards Woefully broken and weak  - Free for all multiplayer loot  On a bright note:  - Background Environment is beautifully rendored  - Excellent Music  All in all, if you are going to purchase this, I would wait until it goes on sale.  $20 or less.  The game is alright as a SP game but no where near worth the full price.  Many people are comparing this to BG1 and BG2, but you will not find the caliber of story as is in BG1 or 2.  Since there is only one avenue that we can compare the DM tools to, just realize that these tools are woefully weaker then the Aurora Toolset released with NWN/NWN2.  Easier to use, but you will never be able to make exactly what you want and with no tile by tile dungeon editing, a static overland map,no mods and no scripting.  The editor most likely will never fully satisfy.  If you are just looking for yet another budget Single Player Game or for a toolset to create quick, simple  Dungeon Runs with Friends, then yes this may be something that intices you, but be forwarned as to the limitations this game has.

Original review: The game could be better labeled as Massive Empire Management Simulator for that is what you do. You babysit your planets, you babysit your starbases, you babysit your fleets. The most crippling amount of micromanagement ever invisionsed in a 4X game. If its vast sprawling empires you want to build while slowly losing your mind trying to keep track of what is where, then this game could very well be perfection. If however you want a challenging and stimulating 4X space  game where you fight fun battles and arent swarmed with endless micromanagement choices then I would recommend Sins of a Solar Empire much more so over this.

Thief of Thieves: Season One: ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~  Your boss is one of the most wanted men in the world; a man who has the reputation of pulling off the most difficult and dangerous heists ever attempted. No one knows his real name, or what he looks like. All we know is that he is referred to as, Redmond the Master Thief. Lucky you, Redmond has taken you under his wing and you’ll travel the world as part of his team, and be involved in the most incredible heists, in Thief of Thieves: Season one!  Thief of Thieves: Season One is an adventure / choice matters game with stealth elements, which was developed and published by Rival Games LTD on the 17 July 2018. This game is based on the comic books created by Robert Kirkman.  The game starts with the protagonist, Celia Kowalczyk (your character), walking through the airport on the way to the exit. Unfortunately for her, she is going to be stopped by an agent for questioning about her last three months’ whereabouts. From here, you’ll be able to play her most recent four robberies, which have between three to five parts each.  Within these sections, you’ll be entertained with a flowing story, great comic illustrations and superb voice-overs. These scenes will occur at the start and throughout the mission.     The missions have a bit of variation, which is fabulous! Most of the mission will involve reconnaissance, planning, hacking devices, pick-pocketing, eaves-dropping on various characters to get information, and conducting the robbery.   There are plenty of interactions throughout the story. Before launching a part of the mission, Celia will be able to talk to other people on her team and choose how the conversation goes, with three to four different options each time she asks questions or talks. On some occasions, she’ll be able to select one of the other team members into the next section of the mission, which is really cool.   In regards to the stealth element, in most sections of the operation, Celia will explore buildings such as a train station, a bank, a cocktail bar, as well as a house in order to complete tasks.  In these sections, she’ll encounter obstacles such as guards and cameras. She’ll also have to figure out how to solve puzzles to successfully clear the episode. The key here is to be patient, study the guard’s movements, be very quiet as she moves around, and to use the shadows as much as possible so as not to be detected. If she is seen, Celia will need to find a place to hide to avoid being caught. Beware, Celia is not the greatest fighter, and it will only take one hit for her to be knocked down. Fortunately, the game has an autosave each time she reaches a key point within the specific section of the mission and will respawn there if she has been caught.  She can also interact with certain objects (which will be highlighted with a dot above) when she walks close by.  Alternatively, she can use the intuition mode by pressing and holding the right button on the mouse, which will show the details of all the possible interactions.  The characters in this game are extremely well-designed in terms of their personality traits, backgrounds, and how they fit in the story, which is full of suspense and twists.   The comic style of graphics and animations are sensational, and I really enjoyed the soundtrack as well. Absolutely spot on voice-over all way through the game. Well balanced gameplay - I was entertained from start to finish!   Positives: ~~~~~~~   +	Great graphics +	Stunning story +	Good soundtrack +	Well-designed characters and traits +	Achievements and trading cards  Negatives: ~~~~~~~~   -	How long do we have to wait for season two?   It is “SAFE” to say, Thief of Thieves: Season one is a “CRACKER” of a game!  9/10  Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own! Vesta: ~~~~~    Some people find themselves in a pickle every now and then. This one is rather large with plenty of challenges ahead, especially if the person is 6 years old. This is Vesta’s predicament; she was woken up by a BOT on the 152nd floor of a deserted underground city, on another planet far from earth with the exciting news that the energy resources are running extremely low. With the help of a BOT and a DROID, she must make her way to the surface, fight various robots and discover what really happened on this planet.   Vesta is a puzzle / adventure game where you control a 6 year-old girl and a DROID. Your goal is to reach the surface of planet OPS by completing 36 levels in 4 chapters.  After a very nice cartoon-style introduction, the first few levels are basically a nicely laid-out tutorial. After learning how to transfer the energy from the multifunctional Energy Transnobbler to the device she has on her back and vice versa, Vesta will be ready to make her way to the upper levels. At the start of the game Vesta will only have the capacity to store one bar of energy in her device. Rest assured she will earn another two storage bars fairly quickly within chapter one.  As for the Transnobblers, they have a base with a green tank on top. Pipes connect the Transnobbler to other structures, such as doors, platforms and travelators. To activate these structures, Vesta has to fill in the empty tanks with the green energy.   The Droid (named Seven) will help her to remove obstacles and other dangerous robots. Seven is armed with some sort of missile which can momentarily freeze enemies and destroy wooden boxes. It can sometimes be a bit tricky to eliminate robots in some levels due to the fact that you must use the droid and Vesta to complete the kill. First use the droid and shoot at the target; as soon as the missile hits the enemy, a clock appears above it and a countdown will start. From here, switch to Vesta, move towards the robot, drain its energy and the kill will be complete. Mind you, there are a few types of robot and some of them have a very fast countdown compared to others, therefore Vesta must be close by to successfully eliminate them. What else can these robots do to make Vesta’s life difficult? The spider robots shoot laser beams in different directions, Bots will fly around trying to catch both Vesta and Seven, others will drop mines and even smash the floors. As Vesta is a child, it will only take her one hit to die while Seven can take three. If one of them dies, you’ll restart the level, or if you manage to reach a round symbol (located on the floor), you’ll restart from there. As Seven is a robot, he is capable of throwing Vesta a short distance, which is extremely useful if there is acid on the floor and your character can’t reach a transnobbler.   They are a couple of other things to do in this game. First, there are secrets to discover; the number of secrets varies depending on each level. The second is about the story which you can read by activating consoles within the stages. I really enjoy the cartoon type of cut-scenes, they are well done and fun to watch. Puzzles-wise, they are pretty easy to complete, as are the bosses’ fights at the end of each chapter.    Graphically, the game looks great and the levels are well-designed. The soundtrack is very nice and the controls work very well. I would recommend using a gamepad rather than the mouse and keyboard. I did experience a few freezes during the loading sequence, which is a bit annoying.  Positives: ~~~~~~~   +	Nice, colourful graphics +	36 Levels to complete +	Great cut-scenes +	Achievements  Negatives: ~~~~~~~~   -	A bit repetitive -	No trading cards as yet  Vesta is a fun puzzle / adventure game for all ages!   7/10  Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Music Band Manager: ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~  Music is a universal joy. There are so many styles to fall in love with throughout the course of our lives, to make us smile, dance, reflect and even dream. These songs or harmonies that become stuck between our two ears for days without missing a beat are played by talented individuals or bands. Have you ever asked yourself how long it took these artists to become famous before performing all around the world at the biggest events? Well, now you have a chance to experience it yourself by creating your own group in Music band Manager!  Music Band Manager is casual management / simulation game where you take control of a group of four musicians and attempt to bring them fame and fortune.   At the start of the game, you’ll have to choose what type of music your band will play. Will it be a Pop, Rock, Hip-hop or Techno?  Whatever style you choose it would just mean that your musicians will have better skill points towards that genre of music at the start of the game. Don’t worry, you’ll be able to train them in the other genres, too.   Straight after that, you’ll proceed to a short tutorial which is well done.   From here it’s totally up to you. The main screen will give you the ability to see the profile of your musicians. You can upgrade their instruments and microphones (for your front man/woman), and give them other items which can help to create better songs faster, increase revenue and other options. You’ll be able to write songs, rehearse, record and sell your songs, and each of them will have sub-options. For example, you’ll be able to choose what type of music each of your musicians will play in a specific training session to help them to increase their knowledge of that style of music. You’ll be able to choose to record with different studios; some will be cheaper, but they’ll produce a record with lower sound quality than more expensive studios. Hiring managers will help bring more fans and opportunities to your group, such as interviews on radio, tv and much more. Each time your manager asks you to do something, you’ll be prompted with three possible responses. Depending on your response, you might gain money, more fans or even additional points towards writing a song with a specific theme which might result in a big hit! Later on in the game, you’ll be able to put together an album, and with a bit of luck it might be rated in the top 200 on the charts!  The second screen is a map showing the cities in which your band can play and how much money they’ll earn per gig. Your first map is Western Europe, which has around 20 venues on the map. However, you’ll only be able to play at one venue until you gain more fame, which will unlock the next venue. Some venues will require that your group has knowledge of a certain genre of music before you can play there, so don’t forget to train your musicians in all styles of music.  Then book your calendar and make money! When all locations are unlocked and you have the right amount of money and fans, you can move your band to another part of the world to increase your revenue and popularity. You’ll need to do this 7 times to reach America. The good news is that your band will be able to go back to the previous region via a tour. Another way to make money is to accept random jobs, but you could risk not being paid.   What you need to make sure of is that you accumulate enough money every 7 days to avoid bankruptcy.   The graphics are nice and colourful and the interface is very easy to use. I was hoping for more variety in terms of the soundtrack, though; there are only a few sounds playing over and over again. As soon as you figure out how to remain in the black each week, it becomes a bit repetitive.  Positives: ~~~~~~~   +	Colourful graphics +	Good tutorial +	Easy to play / good interface +	Good price point +	Achievements and trading cards  Negatives: ~~~~~~~~   -	Needed better soundtrack -	A bit repetitive  Bring the world the biggest music act ever seen, in Music Band Manager!  7/10  Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Follow The Cpt Froggy Club Curator Page for plenty more![/b][/url][/quote]  SteamWorld Quest: Hand of Gilgamech:  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ A long time has passed since the hero Gilgameh defeated the Behemoth with the Heart of Evil, who was created by the gods! Well, that was during the early age of SteamWorld. Since then, nothing drastic has happened in that world. Well, that’s until two friends, a knight and an alchemist, were walking into the forest to find a rare mushroom - a peppermint puffer. The mushroom itself could do wonders for the SteamWorld community, but what was happening close by in a small village was the start of an incredible adventure. The army of a Dark Lord set the village alight, and these two friends would need as much help as possible in the adventure of SteamWorld Quest: Hand of Gilgamech!  SteamWolrd Quest: Hand of Gilgamech is an adventure/card/strategy game developed by Image & Form Games and Published by Thunderful Publishing, and it was released on the 31st of May 2019 on the Steam platform.  Before I start talking about this game, I must say that I am a huge fan of Image Form Games Studio and I had the pleasure of playing all their SteamWorld games so far.  It seems to me that they are getting stronger each time they release a new title, and this one’s an absolute cracker!  The game consists of 19 chapters, each with a boss to defeat. You can choose to play the game in three levels of difficulty (Squire, Knight or Legend). As mentioned, you’ll start with two characters at your disposal, Copernica the Alchemist and Armilly the knight. As you progress in the game, a few more characters will join your party. In my case, after 14 hours of play and having completed 12 chapters, I have another three characters.  The levels are set up as rooms, through which you will move your party. Entering each of the rooms may activate a dialogue between the characters (which you can skip if you want to), but mostly you’ll encounter enemies and go straight into a fight. If you manage to sneak behind them and attack them first, they will take on a small damage before entering the fight. The other rooms will have objects such as books, roots and boxes to smash to pieces, and you’ll be rewarded with coins when destroying some of them. Let me tell you, you’ll need plenty of coins to upgrade and create your deck of cards, as well as for procuring weapons, accessories and other gizmos at the old rusted merchant caravan.  You can only have three characters in a fight but will occasionally face up to five enemies per battle. The fight is set up as a turn-based system and at the start of each battle, you’ll be given 6 cards to choose from. If you use three characters (which you will), you might have 2 cards for each of your characters, but most of the time it’s totally randomized, which is super fun. In each turn, you can choose to replace 2 cards of the six that you have in your hand. Some cards will cost you nothing while others need a certain number of gears to activate.  The gears tab is located at the top of your screen. Each time you select a card without a cost, one of the gears will become orange, which means that you now own one gear. The other way to activate gears is to create a chain of cards. The trick is to activate as many gears as possible to gain access to more powerful cards each turn, but it can be tricky. You see, you can only use three cards per turn. Usually the cards that don’t cost gears inflict low damage to enemies, regenerate a bit of health or sightly improve your armour. If you use three of these cards in one turn, you’ll earn three gears for the next turn and then you can use more powerful cards. If, for instance, you can pick up three cards from one of the characters in a turn, you’ll create a chain which will give you either an extra attack, armour, or health in that turn. So yeah, try to produce these chains of cards as many times as possible.   At the end of each turn, the three cards you used will be replaced by another 3 new cards, and so on and so forth, until you win or loose the battle.  There are items that you can use during a fight, such as repair potion, revive a hero and others. If you need to do so, it will become part of the three you use per turn. Maybe all heroes will need a repair potion at once, and therefore that will become the set of cards for that specific turn.   At the end of each battle, you’ll be rewarded with coins, materials and items.   In each of the levels, you’ll find an old (rusted) merchant with her caravan. There, you’ll be able to buy or sell weapons, accessories, material and recovery Items. You’ll also be able to upgrade your cards or add new cards to the hero’s deck. To do so, you’ll need the right materials and coins.  I really like everything about this game! You have a good story with great humour, the interface is easy to use all way around, and it is challenging, too. On top of that, the graphics are fabulous! If you enjoy adventure, card games and strategy, this game is for you. In my case, I found myself playing the game until the early hours of the morning. It’s a GEM! I love first-person RPGs.  Especially ones where you can craft your character through stats and perks, and play the part you've chosen for them.  So stuff like New Vegas or EYE.  What I do NOT like are games that advertise themselves as these sorts of RPGs and then railroad you into playing a specific part.  Guess which category Fallout 4 falls into?  And yet ... despite the severely limited dialogue checks, the shallow story that forces your character into a specific archetype, the focus on combat over peaceful resolution (even when it seems like peace would be the more logical option), and the sheer rage-inducing plot holes that crop up (honey, do not EVEN get me STARTED on Curie's quest!)...I keep wandering back to the Commonwealth.  Is it the settlement building?  Where the game lacks in depth of choice for characters, it more than makes up for it in depth of choice for base construction.  A wide variety of materials and settings to choose from, and you can truly make a home that is your own.  Is it the DLCs?  Each DLC adds something new to the table, and each is a joy to play.  Automaton adds the addictive robot-building mechanics.  Far Harbor adds actual subtlety and nuance, crafting a thought-provoking story that should've been the main game to begin with.  Nuka World adds a thrilling theme park to explore, and the finally an option to be a prick.  Vault 88 allows you to construct your own vault from the ground up, and maybe stick a middle finger to Vault-Tec in the process.  And the rest of them add more goodies to the settlements, which is nice.  Is it the exploration?  The map is small, but so densely packed with secrets that it feels larger.  Maybe you'll find a new settlement.  Maybe you'll find a Deathclaw.  Maybe you'll find a cool new gun.  Maybe you'll find a ship full of quirky robotic sailors.  Who knows!  Could it be that, despite the lack of traditional RPG immersiveness, Fallout 4 has created a whole new way to become submerged in a game's world?  ...nah, it's gotta be Codsworth. Updating my review for 1.0:  The game has made a ton of progress, but it's still far from perfect. This is one of the few games that is insanely fun despite the plethera of bugs and imperfections. Just to give you an idea of where the game truly shines and where it needs improving, here is a list of pros and cons at it's current state:  *Pros*:  - Beautiful environments and good graphics, lots of areas to explore. - Crafting and loot have been improved, and having decent gear takes roughly 30 mins. - Vitals system (water, food, temp, blood, overall health) works well. - You no longer die from 3 foot falls or broken ladders. - Player encounters can be random and exciting. - Overall much more stable than beta version.  *Cons*:  - Zombies are still somewhat broken, half the time they will stand still once alerted, and I have occasionally been hit inside a building by a zombie, despite them being nowhere near me. - Gun play and pvp feels clunky. - Stuttering and major FPS drops in towns. I have a GTX1070 build and get 144 frames at medium settings outside towns, but once I get into town with other players and zombies, it goes down to about 40. - Still the occasional glitch of getting stuck in a car, underneath a fence, animations not working, etc.  If you can accept the game at it's current state, then get it. But if you want to wait for improvements and a smoother gameplay experience, then save your money for now.

Best Pitch Black Room Simulator of 2015, bar none. Let me tell you.  The best part of the game is that it is aparantly built entirely in Python. All the stability and speed of an interpreted language is on display here. THe server list helpful lists games in alphabetical ascii order, where lowercase a comes after uppercase Z. Can't find game aaron aardvark? that's because it's below Zombie Zoomba. Join a game if you dare!  Imagine you are in a dark room, you can hold up a flash light, that illuminates a narrow cone for you, but no one else can see it. Now imagine crawling around on your hands and knees though a house looking for tiny keys that open random doors. Which keys open which doors? I have no idea, sometimes you get a decription on the key, but the doors have no names. If you are lucky enough to open a door, hold on to the click button and move back and forth a bit until the door physics freaks out and opens in a random direction. Sometimes you hear scary music which means it is action time.  Begin action time. If they are a powerful monster, you are should immediately turn off your flashlight and run in a random direction. You are dead anyway, but this might make them waste 0.03 seconds which might allow one of your friends to escape. If they are a weak monster, turn off your flashlight and run in a random direction. You will sometimes live, beacuse the monster will get caught on a jagged edge and spin in space randomly. Success! Please note, unlike humans, monsters CAN see flashlights. They have monster eyes.  Ok, you have been crawling around lost in the house and/or creepy woods (you can tell it is creepy because there are jack-o-lantern's every 17.2 feet in every hallway, that's how you know it's scary) for a long time, and you have not seen a battery to click on in a while, and OH NOES YOUR BATTERY IS DEAD. Begin pitch dark screen simulator. On the macbook pro it is especailly convincing, because the monitor doesn't even turn on! You are in the pitch dark, you can see nothing, hope is lost, except that it might take the monster another 20 minutes to find you because he has a hard time seeing you because he only sees flashlights (monster eyes). If you are very lucky and at a LAN party and another dead survivor is in the room with you, he can spectate you and you can screenlook on his screen to help you nagivate. Or he can yell directions to you. My friend Jimmy did this for me, Jimmy you are the best.  If you are the monster, life is great, even if you are a bad monster. Walk around randomly. Sometimes a survivor walks in front of you. Turn into a real monster, and click on them. They are dead! Do this 3 more times. You win! Acheivements for everyone! Well, not everyone. Just you. Those poor saps were crwaling on their hands and knees trying to figure out how to open a cabinet with the wierd door physics trying to find a key which may or may not exist for the unlabeled door. Puny scum! Also, half of them probably have crippling graphical glitches, like a serverlist of games to join blocking most of their screen. That's the breaks! After 7 games of the survivors never managing to open more than a few doors, convince the monster to stay put and try to let the survivors win one game. After an hour of trying to find keys with 4 survivors and no monster, turn off game, unable to find door or even begin to understand the win condition. You are a winner!

Persona 4 is an experience that can't really be compared to most other games (Even from a Persona standpoint, it stands tall above the rest for such individualized charming reasons!)  Between engaging dungeon-crawling with fun party setups and planning, you get to enjoy a life in the small-but-cozy town of Inaba where you get to know & connect with deep characters, all of whom have great chemistry with the ingame friend group. These characters really grow on you over the course of a 60+ hour playthrough, and building these bonds is not only satisfying, but crucial to success in the dungeons as well (Your bonds help grow your personas, and your personas help grow your bonds in a really satisfying cycle between RPG and slice-of-life mechanics that are cleverly interwoven). Behind the warm and friendly town, there's a really intriguing murder-mystery to be solved, and every step of the way is satisfying, full of twists, and delivers a powerful payoff. This game is an EXPERIENCE that, for such a low price, everybody deserves to play!

This game mostly lived up to its name, although it feels like it is diverging a little from its original formula. It feels a lot darker and more political than the others, although all Tales games have an edge to them. There is a lot more running around collecting things and backtracking, some of which can get repetitive, where the others have felt a lot more linear up until the end. However, it is still as epic and story driven as the others. The music is okay but some of it felt too ambient and subtle, where I prefer more traditional JRPG music (a problem I also had with Graces at times). The battle system is mostly the same sort of thing but felt a little more awkward than the previous games. Strangely, I found this game easier to control with a keyboard and mouse than a gamepad, despite it being from a long line of console RPGs. The button mashing feels smoother with a mouse. Then again, the series is slowly changing anyway and at least they kept a lot of the important things, like the Katz!

Sleeping Dogs is easily one of the best open world crime sandboxes I've played in a long time. It is a nice blend of the later GTA's grittiness and realism, showing the deep dark underbelly of corruption and crime, while maintaining a slight sense of humor about it, a la Saint's Row. The gameplay isn't exactly that different from any other games of this genere, save for the combat. The melee combat (which you use a lot) is very fluid, making stringing together combos a very rewarding challenge. The somewhat limited gunplay (lampshaded in-game by saying that guns are rare in Hong Kong) is nothing to write home about, yet I still found myself enjoying the occasional gun battle. There are two things which got to me in this game: The story and the graphics. For a game two years old, the graphics blow me away, even on a medium-high setting. The story is the thing that had me hooked on the game the most. As a sufferer of gaming ADD, I found myself unable to pull away from the game! I highly recommend Sleeping Dogs, regardless of the price.

Payday: The Heist is a first person shooter game developed by Overkill Software and published by Sony Entertainment. The game was released in October 2011 on PC, after being released on PS3. The game is owned on Steam by over four million players due to its regularity being on sale.   The gameplay is based around completing heists with a party of four people including you. This can be done either in a single player environment, or up to 4 player co-op online. The heists can consist of the classic bank jobs, right the way to the complete extreme of extracting blood from a highly classified patient. You play the role of one of the four main characters in the game, Dallas, Chains, Wolf or Hoxton.  Each member of the team can use a variety of different weapons, you are able to select your load out before jumping into a heist, so once you get to know what is needed to be done on each heist, you can select what to use accordingly. Each of the missions starts off in a stealth style mission, where you have to disable security camera, turning off alarm systems etc. Whether you complete these tasks successfully or not without being seen will determine how the rest of the heist will carry out.  These starting missions are done really well, and you will be fully immersed since most of them have you sneaking around a pitch black building trying to out manoeuvre the guards. A lot of the missions also come with the added obstacle of civilians – these are crucial in any of the heists as you can keep them hostage and use them as bargaining trades should one of your other team mates be captured by the police too.   Whilst you can spend a good portion of the game in stealth and hopefully not being noticed, a good portion of the game will also be spent with you going all guns blazing as you attempt to fend off an almost endless stream of enemy police and SWAT.  The gunplay in Payday really well done. All of the guns feel as powerful as you would expect, and the choice of weapons is pretty big when compared to other FPS games.  Ammo does become a problem with your primary weapon since you’ll be shooting this off constantly at points, but can be easily countered by the abundance of pickups of ammo off dead enemies.   Even though Payday is almost four years old at this point, it is still a really good looking game, especially when you ramp up the resolution to 4k. Originally I thought the game was made using the Source engine due to the familiarities in the graphics with the likes of Half Life 2 and Left 4 Dead, but the game is made using an engine called Diesel (made by GRIN, who are now defunct unfortunately). There are a couple of textures which are very low resolution which is a shame, but I can forgive this a bit given that a lot of the levels are actually fairly big, so this must have been done to reduce the need for loading screens.  The game has a really good ragdoll simulation too, when you are mowing down the enemies, they don’t just die in a normal fall to the floor fashion, each death is individually animated depending on where/how they were shot, which adds to the originality slightly.   Payday is fully voice acted and done really well at that; the game is almost narrated by what seems to be someone behind the scenes instructing your team on what to do next on the heist. You’ll get remarks back from the rest of the team in responses to objectives being completed and you’ll also get a lot of radio chatter when you are in firefights with the police too.   This is a really hard game. The first couple of heists come with the option to play them on easy mode; these must really be the games tutorial since they can be completed without any real problems; yet once you reach the third or fourth mission, the difficulty takes a big ramp up and you’ll actually find yourself either failing missions from not completing objectives, or because you have died or been taken into custody. I had to replay each of the last few stages of the game multiple times before I was able to successfully complete the heists. Even though the ramp in difficulty felt really harsh at the time; I began to enjoy the game even more because of it; because it’s not just as simple as a “get in and out” job, it forces you to plan your every move, and you will tread with caution around every corner because of the unknown ambush that awaits you. The game also has another two difficulty levels to be played on, Hard and overkill mode – these are modes which should not even be considered when playing on single player because you will not stand a chance. I tried the overkill mode out and it is just absolute carnage. I will definitely be asking friends to join in a game to give this mode a proper try out.   Whilst all of the missions have the same key objective, and there is really only one way to complete said objective, it can lead to a little repetitive gameplay. The game does however try to counteract that by adding a little bit of randomness into the stages by shaking things up a bit; such as locations the locations of key civilians that you need to keep hostage, meaning you still have to go searching through the whole building to find them rather than rushing to the one place. Each of the levels has some form of random element to it which is nice to see, since you will be playing the same six or seven heists over and over again.  I have put about twenty hours into Payday: The Heist so far and see no end in sight for it at the moment. There is still a really active multiplayer scene if you want to just find pick up groups with randommers, but I would highly recommend playing this with a bunch of friends on Skype to get the full experience out of it. The added levels of difficulty also adds plenty of replay ability too; meaning you will not run out of interesting content for a long while with this title. The game does have one piece of DLC which includes new weapons and two new heists, which is a worthwhile piece of DLC.   The game is also extremely technically sound too; I was able to play on 4k resolution with all of the graphic options maxed out and I was still able to hit the heights of 160 FPS, so this is one of the best optimized games out there at the moment.  Keyboard and mouse is recommended to play with, given the FPS nature.  Overall, Payday: The Heist is an extremely good game; one that I am surprised it has taken me so long to play, and one that I will certainly be keeping installed on my machine because of the high replay ability factor. The game is also very cheaply priced at £10,99 – but like I said at the start, the game is always going on sale, and most of the time it is for 90% off; at that price, is it an absolute no brainer to pick it up – you may as well pick up the four pack for yourself and friends whilst you are at it. [h1]This game was reviewed using a code sent by the developer.[/h1]  Guns, Gore & Cannoli is a a side scrolling action shooter with the welcome addition of zombies. This game was released in April 2015 and has actually got a surprisingly low number of owners given how awesome it is. You play the role of a gangster named Vinnie. You are thrown into Thugtown to find another gangster who has gone missing. You soon find the town has been overrun by zombies as you wade your way through streets, buildings, sewers and urban America.  This is one of the best side scroller games of this type; it's action packed and face paced. Gunplay is a key factor, with about 8 or 9 different weapons which you will eventually find, you have plenty in your arsenal. Whilst working your way through the levels, you will find health packs in the form of Cannoli and tons of ammo to keep you rolling. All of the weapons have their own feel and different uses and none of them feel useless.  There are a couple of jumping type puzzles in the latter levels, but the platforming element of the game is very limited.   The art style in Guns, Gore & Cannoli is gorgeous. The cartoon magazine style look really works well with the setting and story. Not to mention all of the animations are perfectly done too. I often find problems with games that have a generic cartoon look, but this is easily one of the best games to pull it off.   Guns, Gore & Cannoli also has some very nicely recorded voice acting; the American/Italian accent feels like it has just come straight off the streets of New York. Hats off to these devs who put in the extra work for the voice acting, as they could of quite easily just put in text instead, for me it made the game so much more enjoyable.   This game has a very gentle difficulty curve, I only really struggled with the last couple of levels of the game, but was able to push on through once the best weapon was chosen for the scenario. The end boss is also quite challenging too which is a refreshing change compared to other games nowadays.  At some points trying to kill everything on site is not always the best option too; sometimes you just need to run and hope that there is a checkpoint near by because you are just being overrun - keep that in mind.   Length wise, I completed the game in just under three hours on single player. Whilst there is no real need to replay it again, there are also plenty of achievements for you to go back and hunt, and this can be done easily though the Chapter select option. Guns, Gore & Cannoli also has a local co-op feature too, I have yet to try it out but have watched a couple of Youtube videos of it; and it looks so much fun. This is going to be one of those games that I sit down and play with my partner and finish it for a second time.   I had one technical issue whilst playing; sometimes the game would freeze for half a second. This seems to happen especially when reaching save points; but also happens at random points too. This is a known problem with the game and has been reported to the devs. It seems to point to an issue with the fact that the game records lots of stats, such as headshots etc.   In conclusion; Guns, Gore & Cannoli is a really nicely put together game, and one that needs to be experienced by more people than it already has. For the none sale price of £6,99, this is a bargain to pick up especially if you have friends to play with. LEGO Worlds is a sandbox game developed by Traveller’s Tale and published by Warner Brothers Interactive Entertainment, releasing on Steam in early access in June 2015. The game is still in Early Access and whilst the developers seem to be updating the game on a monthly basis, what they do update isn’t exactly ground breaking stuff and nothing is on the horizon for resolving the issues this game has currently.  Now, followers of my reviews will know I absolutely love LEGO games but sandbox games is probably one of my least favourite genres so I was a little sceptical going into this title but I hoped the LEGO name would carry it a little.   Gameplay wise, there actually isn’t that much to do sadly. You are parachuted into a randomly generated world using a seed system and you will encounter other Lego figures, creatures, items and vehicles. Once you encounter them, they will be “unlocked” – this will allow you to purchase said item using bolt bricks which you pick up by destroying objects in the world or by slaying enemies.  That’s it – there isn’t any crafting system, no little objectives to complete, no story, quests, nothing, just an open world with very little interaction in it. This left me very disappointed as other LEGO games are known for having exciting open worlds and little Easter eggs here and there.   The other game play element is the building mode, which is essentially the creative mode from games like Minecraft.  This was the feature I was most looking to trying out, I had craved a game where you have unlimited bricks that allowed you to just play LEGOs digitally. Minecraft was often referred to as digital LEGO when it first released, now we have just that. Let me start with the plus points of this mode; you have all the tools to build absolutely anything you want; the huge amount of different types of bricks you have at your disposal is impressive. LEGO Worlds also has a very good terrain controlling tool, much like Minecraft has but it is far better designed and you can modify your world without causing your PC to grind to a halt. Sadly these plusses are marred with the game’s biggest fault – the controls and camera.  The camera in this game is absolutely atrocious; it prevents you from having any sort of enjoyment out of the anything! Because you have such a large selection of small Lego Bricks to use when constructing your models, you obviously need to be very precise with your placement of bricks, the camera does everything and anything it can to prevent that and just ends up jumping all over the shop, not moving where you ask it to, or just plain and simply not working at all. This made the game unplayable and left me very salty.   Graphically the game is made out of Lego bricks, but there is so much visual noise on screen as literally everything is made out of bricks so all the walls and mountains are built piece by piece out of small individual bricks, which can be a little off putting when you are looking out over the world. It almost comes across as being a little pixelated which some may find distasteful.  I would have liked to see it take on the same style that the other LEGO games use, where objects are built using bricks, but the actual environment has a sort of split between bricks and normal material. The music is also fairly off putting too; it doesn’t fit the LEGO universe at all, I felt like I was marching into battle at times, it is very regimental and just not right for this type of game.   I’ve been playing LEGO Worlds for just about two hours now and I feel like I actually wanted to stop playing way before now.  This would easily be one of my favourite games if I could actually play it, I would be able to spend hours upon hours in this game just playing LEGOs – this is the sort of game that you could easily introduce small children to playing if it wasn’t so damn hard to control.   Apart from the technical problems with the camera, I also had slight performance problems too. Even on my rig I wasn’t able to get a steady 60 fps. This isn’t a rare problem either, after checking the forums people with much beefier rigs than mine were also experiencing performance problems of not even being able to breach the 30 fps mark which is absolutely absurd for the hardware being used.   This game is quite obviously in no state both technically and mechanically to be considered a worthy purchase right now. I am astounded this has been marked as “Very positive” for overall reviews because it is just unplayable. I seriously hope the devs are able to fix the problems with the camera as I really would love to play this game some more, but right now it is not worth your time or money.  It has all the potential to be a really good creative game, not so much on the “survival” side but to use it as a tool to just build LEGOs till your hearts content. I am going to rate this as a not recommended for now.
